opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the main value of the paper is that it raises a question that people haven't really been asking, which is: what's actually going on *inside* these networks, regardless of how well they perform on the outside?

There's a kind of implicit optimism in deep learning, which is what we're calling representational optimism. The assumption is that if you scale up, get more data, and the loss goes down and the benchmarks go up, then the internal representation must be getting better too. Performance is treated as a proxy for the quality of the underlying representation. What we tried to show is that this assumption isn't necessarily true. You can get the exact same output, the same behavior, and still have a completely different and much worse representation underneath.

The way we showed this is a bit unusual, and I think that's part of what makes it valuable. We went back to Picbreeder, the old interactive evolution experiment where people bred images over many generations without a predetermined goal. Some of the networks that came out of that process have remarkable internal structure. Take the famous skull image. If you look inside the network, you find what we call a unified, factored representation. There are individual weights that do semantically meaningful things, like opening and closing the mouth, or the symmetry of the face showing up as a real, clean decomposition. The network seems to understand the skull in a deep sense, even though nobody was trying to make a skull when the process started.

Then we took the same image and trained a network of the same kind with conventional SGD to reproduce it exactly. The output is basically pixel-perfect. But when you look inside, it's a mess. The representation is what we call fractured and entangled. Things that should be one concept get split into disconnected pieces, and things that should be separate get tangled together. If you perturb the weights, you don't get a mouth opening, you get garbage. So it looks the same from the outside, but it's like a fake underneath. It's an imposter, in a sense.

Why does that matter? Because I think the quality of representation is going to matter a lot for what we care about beyond benchmark performance: generalization to genuinely new situations, creativity, continual learning, the ability to build on what you know. If a model's understanding is fractured, it might perform beautifully on the distribution it was trained on, but its ability to make meaningful creative leaps or adapt in a principled way could be quite compromised. And we might not notice, because we only measure the outputs.

So I see the paper as a kind of provocation, or an existence proof. It doesn't say large models are worthless, and it doesn't claim we fully know how FER manifests in large language models. But it does say we shouldn't just assume that good performance means good representation. It opens a research direction about how to detect this, how to measure it, and, maybe most interestingly, how open-ended, non-objective processes like the one in Picbreeder led to such better representations. That connects back to a lot of what I've been saying for years about objectives and open-endedness, but now there's a very concrete, visual example of why it might matter.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts SGD with Picbreeder, but does not explain that an apparently troubling SGD representation alone cannot establish a defect without a comparison baseline.

r002.rationale: It identifies the distinctive comparison: an SGD-trained network with a fractured, entangled representation versus Picbreeder’s more unified, factored representation.

r003.rationale: It describes the paper as raising an overlooked question about what happens inside networks and opening research into detecting and measuring representational flaws.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the main value is really about raising a question that I don't think the field has been asking enough, which is: what is actually going on inside these networks, and should we assume that just because a network performs well on its task, the representation underneath that performance is good? There's this kind of implicit optimism in the field that scaling and gradient descent are going to give us good representations as a side effect of getting good behavior. And what we're saying is, maybe not. Maybe what's happening is that you get the behavior you want, but the internal representation is what we call fractured and entangled, which means that the same underlying concept is being represented in multiple disconnected places, and things that should be separate are kind of tangled up together in a way that doesn't reflect the actual structure of the problem.

The way we got there is actually kind of fun. We looked at networks that were trained to produce the exact same output, so the same image, in two very different ways. One was through conventional SGD, just backprop on the target. And the other was through an open-ended evolutionary process, the kind of thing people built in Picbreeder, where humans were selecting images over many generations without any fixed target in mind. And the outputs are basically identical, you can't tell them apart. But when you look inside, the networks are radically different. The evolved ones have this beautiful, modular, almost interpretable structure where if you sweep a single weight, you get something meaningful, like the mouth of a skull opens and closes, or the eyes move together. And in the SGD-trained network, when you sweep a weight, you get noise. You get garbage. It's like the concepts just aren't there as units.

So the value, I'd say, is twofold. One is just making people aware that this distinction exists, that there's a difference between a good representation and a representation that happens to produce the right answer. And two, that this probably matters for a lot of things we care about, like generalization, creativity, continual learning. If your representation is fractured and entangled, it's going to be harder to learn new things on top of it without breaking what's already there, and harder to generalize gracefully. And I think the hopeful part is that it suggests there's a lot of headroom. If we found a way to get representations more like the evolved ones at scale, we might get a lot of these properties that people are currently trying to get through brute force.

r001.rationale: The response compares SGD-trained networks with evolved ones, but does not say that SGD representations’ troubling appearance alone is insufficient to establish a defect or that a baseline is needed.

r002.rationale: It identifies the comparison between SGD-trained representations and evolved representations, describing the latter as modular and interpretable.

r003.rationale: It describes the paper’s main value as raising a question the field has not asked enough: whether successful task performance implies good internal representations.

astra-6.text:
I think the main value is to question an assumption that’s so natural in deep learning that we often don’t even articulate it: if we train a network to perform well, then somewhere inside it, it will develop the representations we need for broader intelligence. That’s what we’re calling representational optimism. And the question is whether success on the training objective really justifies that optimism.

The fractured entangled representation hypothesis offers a different possibility. What looks to us like one coherent concept might be fractured across many different contexts in the network. And the things we’d like to treat as separate concepts might be entangled with one another. So a system could perform impressively without organizing what it knows in a way that makes it easy to recombine, extend, or apply in a different situation.

The point isn’t that we’ve established that deep learning can’t work. It’s a hypothesis, and I think its value is in making this alternative explicit. It gives us something to investigate beyond whether the benchmark score went up. Are we getting representations that support further discovery, or are we getting increasingly effective solutions whose internal organization makes certain kinds of generalization difficult? Those are different questions, and I think we need to ask both.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether training success supports broader intelligence, but does not say that troubling appearances alone cannot establish a defect without a baseline for comparison.

r002.rationale: It presents fractured, entangled representations as an alternative hypothesis, but does not describe comparing SGD-derived representations with a more intuitively organized alternative representation.

r003.rationale: It says the hypothesis makes an alternative explicit and gives researchers something to investigate, including whether learned representations hinder recombination, extension, or generalization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main value is making an assumption explicit that we often take for granted: that as these networks get better at their training tasks, their internal representations will become increasingly coherent and useful for understanding the world. That’s what we’re calling representational optimism. And success on a benchmark doesn’t necessarily establish that.

The alternative we’re raising is that a representation can be fractured—different instances of what we would regard as the same concept aren’t necessarily brought together—and entangled, so that the factors we’d like to reason about independently aren’t cleanly separable. A system can still perform impressively with a representation like that. But there may be consequences for how reliably it generalizes or how easily it can build on what it already knows.

So I wouldn’t frame the paper as proving that deep learning cannot work. It’s a hypothesis that challenges a particular explanation of why it works and where continued progress will lead. The value is to open that question up: are we actually getting the kind of representations we think we’re getting, and what evidence would distinguish that from a system that achieves similar performance through something much more fractured and entangled?

r001.rationale: The response does not say that troubling appearances in SGD-derived representations need a baseline for comparison.

r002.rationale: It presents fractured and entangled representations as an alternative hypothesis, but does not compare SGD-derived representations with a more intuitively organized alternative.

r003.rationale: It says the paper opens questions about representation quality and evidence, but does not communicate that these research questions were previously unavailable.
